newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazilian chocolate demand feels post-boom pinch.
newsitem.headline: Brazilian chocolate demand feels post-boom pinch.

text.p: Brazilians have chomped through record amounts of chocolate since 1994, spurred on by an economic plan which has provided the means to satisfy cravings, but a recent slowdown in the economy is taking its toll.

After soaring more than 30 percent in two years, Brazilian chocolate production in 1996 reached 296,300 tonnes, up just 0.9 percent from the previous year and well below earlier hopes of 308,000 tonnes, officials said.
"This is practically zero growth," said Dirceo Campera, co-ordinator at the Brazilian Association of Chocolate, Cocoa, Sweets and Derivatives (Abicab).

Brazilian chocolate consumption was given a strong boost by the anti-inflationary "real" plan launched by the government in July 1994 which finally produced economic stability after years of hyper-inflation.
As a result of the greater demand, production in 1994 jumped to 251,000 tonnes from 220,000 tonnes in 1993, then surged further to 293,700 tonnes in 1995.
One of the key signs of this recovery has been the rebirth of the Easter egg market, with Brazil now in second place behind the U.K. in the world league of Easter egg consumers.

Brazilians have also been drawn to the "exotic", with around 30,000 tonnes of foreign goodies such as Ferrero Rocher and Kinder eggs imported in 1996, up 50 percent from 19,000 tonnes in 1995, Campera said.
But even with the imports, per capita consumption actually fell last year to 1.815 kgs from 1.885 kgs in 1995 because of the growth in population, he added.
"We believe following the boom caused by the "real" plan, people are thinking more carefully about how they spend their money, are more concerned about issues such as unemployment," Campera said.
The outlook for 1997 already looks far from sweet.
At the end of 1996, Abicab had been hoping for chocolate output to rise to around 327,000 tonnes this year.
But if trends seen in January to June continue throughout the year, there may even be a fall in chocolate production in 1997 as consumers count their pennies more, he added.
"Up until July last year I would say we were working at full capacity. Since then however I think industries are working two normal shifts," he said.
The chocolate market is dominated by three companies, Brazil's Garoto, the Brazilian arm of Swiss food giant Nestle SA and Lacta, a Philip Morris Cos Inc company.

According to the Nielsen market research survey, the three companies accounted for around 88 percent of total market share in April and May of this year, said Felipe Buckup, Nestle's chocolate group manager in Brazil.
While there may be a slow-down in demand in 1997, manufacturers believe consumption will soon bounce back and continue to grow at least in line with the country's economy.
"This year we are seeing problems in growth....Consumers have a lot of debts, they are paying off fridges, televisions, etc," said Jacob Cremasco, commercial director at Garoto.
"But the tendency is to have a small fall and afterwards, demand should stabilise and grow at a small rate, probably about the same as GDP," he added.
